CVE-2025-58183.description: tar.Reader does not set a maximum size on the number of sparse region data blocks in GNU tar pax 1.0 sparse files. A maliciously-crafted archive containing a large number of sparse regions can cause a Reader to read an unbounded amount of data from the archive into memory. When reading from a compressed source, a small compressed input can result in large allocations.

CVE-2025-64507.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. An issue ...
CVE-2025-64507.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. An issue in versions prior to 6.0.6 and 6.19.0 affects any Incus user in an environment where an unprivileged user may have root access to a container with an attached custom storage volume that has the `security.shifted` property set to `true` as well as access to the host as an unprivileged user. The most common case for this would be systems using `incus-user` with the less privileged `incus` group to provide unprivileged users with an isolated restricted access to Incus. Such users may be able to create a custom storage volume with the necessary property (depending on kernel and filesystem support) and can then write a setuid binary from within the container which can be executed as an unprivileged user on the host to gain root privileges. A patch for this issue is expected in versions 6.0.6 and 6.19.0. As a workaround, permissions can be manually restricted until a patched version of Incus is deployed.

CVE-2026-115377.description: Incus before 6.0.7, 6.1.0 before 7.0.2, and 7.1.0 before 7.5.0 contains an arbitrary file write vulnerability that allows malicious migration sources to write host files by planting symlinks in transferred volumes. CVE-2026-23953.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-23953.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions 6.20.0 and below, a user with the ability to launch a container with a custom YAML configuration (e.g a member of the ‘incus’ group) can create an environment variable containing newlines, which can be used to add additional configuration items in the container’s lxc.conf due to newline injection. This can allow adding arbitrary lifecycle hooks, ultimately resulting in arbitrary command execution on the host. Exploiting this issue on IncusOS requires a slight modification of the payload to change to a different writable directory for the validation step (e.g /tmp). This can be confirmed with a second container with /tmp mounted from the host (A privileged action for validation only). A fix is planned for versions 6.0.6
and 6.21.0, but they have not been released at the time of publication.

CVE-2026-23954.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Versions ...
CVE-2026-23954.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Versions 6.21.0 and below allow a user with the ability to launch a container with a custom image (e.g a member of the ‘incus’ group) to use directory traversal or symbolic links in the templating functionality to achieve host arbitrary file read, and host arbitrary file write. This ultimately results in arbitrary command execution on the host. When using an image with a metadata.yaml containing templates, both the source and target paths are not checked for symbolic links or directory traversal. This can also be exploited in IncusOS. A fix is planned for versions 6.0.6 and 6.21.0, but they have not been released at the time of publication.

CVE-2026-33542.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33542.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 6.23.0, a lack of validation of the image fingerprint when downloading from simplestreams image servers opens the door to image cache poisoning and under very narrow circumstances exposes other tenants to running attacker controlled images rather than the expected one. Version 6.23.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-33711.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus pr ...
CVE-2026-33711.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus provides an API to retrieve VM screenshots. That API relies on the use of a temporary file for QEMU to write the screenshot to which is then picked up and sent to the user prior to deletion. As versions prior to 6.23.0 use predictable paths under /tmp for this, an attacker with local access to the system can abuse this mechanism by creating their own symlinks ahead of time. On the vast majority of Linux systems, this will result in a "Permission denied" error when requesting a screenshot. That's because the Linux kernel has a security feature designed to block such attacks, `protected_symlinks`. On the rare systems with this purposefully disabled, it's then possible to trick Incus intro truncating and altering the mode and permissions of arbitrary files on the filesystem, leading to a potential denial of service or possible local privilege escalation. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-33743.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33743.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 6.23.0, a specially crafted storage bucket backup can be used by an user with access to Incus' storage bucket feature to crash the Incus daemon. Repeated use of this attack can be used to keep the server offline causing a denial of service of the control plane API. This does not impact any running workload, existing containers and virtual machines will keep operating. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-33897.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33897.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 6.23.0, instance template files can be used to cause arbitrary read or writes as root on the host server. Incus allows for pongo2 templates within instances which can be used at various times in the instance lifecycle to template files inside of the instance. This particular implementation of pongo2 within Incus allowed for file read/write but with the expectation that the pongo2 chroot feature would isolate all such access to the instance's filesystem. This was allowed such that a template could theoretically read a file and then generate a new version of said file. Unfortunately the chroot isolation mechanism is entirely skipped by pongo2 leading to easy access to the entire system's filesystem with root privileges. Version 6.23.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-33945.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus in ...
CVE-2026-33945.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus instances have an option to provide credentials to systemd in the guest. For containers, this is handled through a shared directory. Prior to version 6.23.0, an attacker can set a configuration key named something like `systemd.credential.../../../../../../root/.bashrc` to cause Incus to write outside of the `credentials` directory associated with the container. This makes use of the fact that the Incus syntax for such credentials is `systemd.credential.XYZ` where `XYZ` can itself contain more periods. While it's not possible to read any data this way, it's possible to write to arbitrary files as root, enabling both privilege escalation and denial of service attacks. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-35527.title: Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In ...
CVE-2026-35527.description:
Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In versions prior to 7.0.0, the image import flow issues an outbound HEAD request to a user-supplied URL before validating the request against project restrictions such as restricted.images.servers. The imgPostURLInfo function constructs and sends a HEAD request directly from the attacker-supplied source URL to resolve image metadata, and this network interaction occurs before the flow reaches the point where the import would be rejected by policy. Although the actual image download is blocked by the project restriction, an authenticated user can coerce the daemon into making blind HEAD requests to arbitrary destinations.

These requests include server metadata in custom headers (Incus-Server-Architectures, Incus-Server-Version), which discloses information about the host environment to the attacker-controlled endpoint. This blind SSRF primitive can be used to probe internal services, unroutable address space, or cloud metadata endpoints reachable from the host.

This vulnerability pattern is similar to CVE-2026-24767. This issue has been fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40195.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-40195.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, missing validation logic in the storage bucket import logic allows an authenticated user with access to the storage bucket feature to cause the Incus daemon to crash. The vulnerability is present in the backup metadata handling logic, where the daemon processes the index.yaml file from an imported archive and accesses members of the parsed backup configuration without first verifying that the configuration object was initialized. A malicious or malformed index.yaml that omits the config block causes a nil-pointer dereference during bucket import operations and terminates the daemon. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40197.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-40197.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, missing validation logic in the storage volume import logic allows an authenticated user with access to the storage volume feature to cause the Incus daemon to crash. The custom volume backup import subsystem contains a nil-pointer dereference vulnerability during import operations. In the snapshot import loop, the daemon iterates over entries from `srcBackup.Config.VolumeSnapshots` and assumes that each slice element is initialized, then dereferences fields such as `Name`, `Config`, `Description`, `CreatedAt`, and `ExpiresAt` without first validating the element itself. Because the yaml unmarshaler accepts explicit null array elements from an attacker-controlled index.yaml and converts them into nil pointers inside the slice, an attacker can supply a backup archive containing a null entry in the volume_snapshots array. This causes a nil-pointer dereference during custom volume import and terminates the daemon, resulting in denial of service on the affected node. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40243.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-40243.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, broken TLS validation logic in the OVN database connection logic can allow connections to an attacker's OVN database. The OVN client implementations disable Go standard TLS server verification and replace it with custom peer-certificate verification logic. That replacement verifier does not anchor trust in the configured CA certificate. Instead, it constructs the verification root set from certificates supplied by the peer during the handshake, so the configured CA is parsed but not used as the trust anchor for the final verification decision.

In OVN-enabled deployments that use these SSL database connection paths, an attacker able to impersonate or intercept the OVN endpoint on the management network can present a rogue self-signed certificate chain, and Incus will accept this certificate as valid. This issue defeats the intended CA-based trust model for OVN database connections and permits endpoint impersonation by an active attacker in a suitable network position. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40251.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-40251.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, missing validation logic in the storage volume import logic allows an authenticated user with access to the storage volume feature to cause the Incus daemon to crash. The backup restore subsystem contains an out-of-bounds panic vulnerability caused by an invalid bounds check when indexing snapshot metadata arrays, and the same flawed pattern also appears in the migration path. When iterating through physical snapshots provided in a backup archive, the loop uses the index to look up corresponding metadata in the parsed `Config.Snapshots` and `Config.VolumeSnapshots` slices. The guard condition `len(slice) >= i-1` is incorrect because it can still evaluate to true when the subsequent slice[i] access is out of bounds.

An attacker can submit a backup archive that contains physical snapshot directories while supplying a tampered `index.yaml` with an empty or truncated snapshot metadata array, causing the daemon to index beyond the end of the metadata slice and crash. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-41647.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-41647.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.0.0, a missing error handling could lead an authenticated Incus user to cause a daemon crash through the import of a truncated storage bucket backup file. This issue has been patched in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-41648.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-41648.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.0.0, user provided image and backup tarballs would be unpacked and YAML files parsed without any size restrictions. This was making it easy for an authenticated user to provide a crafted image or backup tarball that when parsed by Incus would lead to a very large YAML document being loaded into memory, potentially causing the entire server to run out of memory. This issue has been patched in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-41684.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-41684.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.0.0, backup.GetInfo() trusts the inline backup/index.yaml config when present and only falls back to parsing the legacy backup/container/backup.yaml file if result.Config == nil. As a result, an archive can carry a valid inline config that passes the initial import preflight while also carrying a malformed legacy backup/container/backup.yaml file that is reparsed later from the restored file system. ParseConfigYamlFile() accepts YAML documents with no container section, and multiple downstream consumers then dereference. Container without checking for nil. Confirmed examples in the instance restore and import flow include backup.UpdateInstanceConfig() and internalImportFromBackup(). An authenticated user with permission to import instance backups may be able to crash the Incus daemon with a crafted backup archive whose inline backup/index.yaml is valid but whose extracted legacy backup.yaml omits container. The crash occurs in the restore path after archive extraction has begun. This issue has been patched in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-41685.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-41685.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.0.0, uploads of large amount of data by authenticated users can run the Incus server out of disk space, potentially taking down the host system. The impact here is limited for anyone using storage.images_volume and storage.backups_volume as those users will have large uploads be stored on those volumes rather than directly on the host filesystem. This is the default behavior on IncusOS. This issue has been patched in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-47753.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-47753.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.1.0, `(*backend).CreateInstanceFromBackup` in `internal/server/storage/backend.go` contains a nil-pointer dereference that an authenticated user with permission to create instances in any project can trigger remotely by uploading a crafted backup tarball. The Incus daemon panics and the process crashes, causing denial of service to every project on that cluster member. This is a sibling of `GHSA-fwj8-62r8-8p8m`, `GHSA-r7w7-mmxr-47r9`, and `GHSA-x5r6-jr56-89pv` (all assigned 2026-05-04). Those patches added guards on adjacent fields of the same `backup/config.Config` struct; the `Volume` field on the instance-import path was missed. Version 7.1.0 contains an updated patch.

CVE-2026-48749.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48749.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, a specially crafted image can be used to read or create/write arbitrary files on the host; possibly leading to arbitrary command execution. Version 7.2.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-48750.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48750.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, the `record-output` parameter of the `/instances/$name/exec` endpoint stores the output of the command in the `exec-output` directory of the instance. If `exec-output` is a symlink, file named `exec_UUID.stdout` and `exec_UUID.stderr` can be written to an arbitrary location where the `.stdout` file will contain arbitrary content. This behavior can be abused for arbitrary command execution. Version 7.2.0 contains a patch.

CVE-2026-48751.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48751.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, instance snapshots ignore the `restricted.containers.lowlevel=block` setting; allowing for arbitrary command execution on the Incus server by abusing lowlevel hooks such as `raw.lxc` and `raw.qemu`. Version 7.2.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-48752.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48752.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, a specially crafted image or instance backup can be used to read or create/write arbitrary files on the host; possibly leading to arbitrary command execution. Version 7.2.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-48753.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48753.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.1.0, the S3 protocol upload endpoint is vulnerable to path traversal and allows creation of arbitrary files on the host. This behavior could lead to arbitrary command execution. Version 7.1.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-48755.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48755.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.1.0, improper validation of user-provided backup compression algorithm leads to argument injection in the constructed command line. This leads to an arbitrary file write on the host, possibly leading to arbitrary command execution. Version 7.1.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-48756.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48756.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.1.0, `(*backend).CreateCustomVolumeFromBackup` in `internal/server/storage/backend.go` contains an unguarded `*time.Time` dereference on the `ExpiresAt` field of every volume-snapshot entry in an imported custom-volume backup. An authenticated user with `can_create_storage_volumes` permission on any project can crash the `incusd` daemon by uploading a backup tarball whose `volume_snapshots[*].expires_at` field is absent. This is a sibling-field variant of GHSA-r7w7-mmxr-47r9 (CVE-2026-40197). Commit `985a1dedf9f3e7ba729c93b654905ed510de25c2` added `if s == nil` at the top of the loop body, but did not guard the adjacent `*snapshot.ExpiresAt` deref 19 lines later. Every other consumer of `Config.VolumeSnapshots[i].ExpiresAt` in this same file already gates the deref with a nil-check — the asymmetric guard is the bug. Version 7.1.0 contains an updated patch.

CVE-2026-48769.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-48769.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, an arbitrary file write exists in the Incus client when a malicious image server returns a crafted `Incus-Image-Hash` header. This can lead to arbitrary command execution as root on the server. Version 7.2.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-55621.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-55621.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, missing authorization checks exist for custom volume copying where an attacker knowing the name of a project that they don't have access to and the name of a custom volume in that project can copy the custom volume to a new project. This issue could allow an attacker to access secrets in custom volumes they are not authorized to access. Version 7.2.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-55622.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-55622.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.2.0, missing authorization checks exist for instance copying where an attacker knowing the name of a project that they don't have access to and the name of an instance in that project can copy the instance to a new project. This issue could allow an attacker to access secrets in instances they are not authorized to access. Version 7.2.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-62313.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-62313.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, project-level enforcement of `restricted.containers.privilege=isolated` can be trivially bypassed, allowing a user to create a non-isolated (shared host idmap) container in a project that is configured to forbid them. The restriction only rejects an explicitly set `security.idmap.isolated=false` (or empty) and fails to enforce anything when the key is omitted entirely. Because an unset `security.idmap.isolated` defaults to `false` (non-isolation), a user simply leaves the key out and obtains exactly the container state the restriction is meant to forbid. This defeats the tenant-isolation guarantee the restriction exists to provide. Containers in the project share the host uid/gid map instead of receiving unique, non-overlapping ranges, weakening the isolation boundary between co-tenant containers and the host. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-62867.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-62867.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. This allows a project-scoped user to inject arbitrary arguments into the binary executed as root. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-62940.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-62940.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, when migrating an instance to another cluster member, user-supplied configuration overrides (including security-critical keys like `security.privileged` and `raw.lxc`) are applied without any project restriction enforcement, allowing a restricted project user to escalate to a privileged container and escape to the host. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-62941.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-62941.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, when copying an instance across projects, the project restriction check (`AllowInstanceCreation`) runs BEFORE the source instance's configuration is merged into the request. Dangerous configuration keys (including `security.privileged`, `raw.lxc`, `raw.apparmor`) from the source instance are merged AFTER the check passes, bypassing all project restrictions on the target project. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-63125.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-63125.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, an unprivileged, project-confined Incus user (a non-admin TLS/RBAC identity with `can_create_images` and `can_create_instances`) can execute arbitrary code as root on the host. A crafted image ships `backup.yaml` as a symlink to a host file. When the root daemon writes the instance's backup file, it follows the symlink. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-63343.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-63343.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, a malicious image containing a `metadata.yaml` symlink pointing to an arbitrary host path allows an authenticated Incus user to read or overwrite any file on the host as root via the instance metadata API. The `exec-output` and `templates/` paths were patched in a prior release using `Lstat` rejection and `os.OpenRoot` confinement; `metadata.yaml` was not included in either patch and remains exploitable. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-81497.title: Arbitrary host file read+write via VM template path traversal (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48752)
CVE-2026-81497.description: ### Summary The fix for **CVE-2026-48752** (`GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479`, template-traversal to host read/write, addressed in **7.2.0**) was applied to the **LXC container driver only**. The sibling **QEMU/VM driver's** template path (`driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`) never received the same guard, so its template read and write remain unbounded. An authenticated user who can **create/launch a VM from a custom image**, or **restore a VM backup**, controls the image/backup `metadata.yaml` (the `templates` map and each `tpl.Template` value) and can traverse out of the templates directory to: - **read arbitrary host files** as root, which are then disclosed into the guest, and - **create root-owned files anywhere on the host** (with a `.out` suffix). ### Details The **LXC driver** was hardened for CVE-2026-48752 (`internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go`): ```go os.OpenRoot(d.RootfsPath()) // ~:7493 confines writes if filepath.Base(tpl.Template) != tpl.Template // ~:7515 rejects any '/', blocks all '../' os.Lstat(d.TemplatesPath()) ... ModeSymlink // ~:7519 / ~:7533 rejects symlinked dir/source ``` The **QEMU/VM driver received none of these**. `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow` (func @ `:3712`) has, before its file operations, only a `slices.Contains(tpl.When, trigger)` check. There is **no path validation**: ```go // READ ~:3779 -- raw tpl.Template, no containment tplString, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(d.TemplatesPath(), tpl.Template)) // WRITE ~:3765 -- raw tpl.Template, path is host-side under incusd (root) w, err = os.Create(filepath.Join(path, fmt.Sprintf('%s.out', tpl.Template))) ``` - **READ vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/shadow'` reads an arbitrary host file, which is rendered into the VM config drive (`config/files/*.out`, exported to the guest over 9p/virtiofs) → **host-file disclosure to the attacker's guest**. Cleanest, exact-path vector. - **WRITE vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/cron.d/x'` creates `/etc/cron.d/x.out`, a **root-owned file anywhere on the host** with pongo2-rendered content. A grep for `os.OpenRoot` / `OpenTemplates` over the templates directory in the incus QEMU path returns **zero hits**. Reachability: `templateApplyNow` is invoked from `generateConfigShare` on **VM start**, so the static call path is strong. **Reference remediation.** Apply incus's own LXC-driver guards (the `filepath.Base` reject + `os.OpenRoot` confinement) to `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`, covering both the read and the write. For the **read** specifically, upstream **LXD** is a second reference (it confines the QEMU read via `d.OpenTemplates()`, an `os.Root`). Note that **LXD does *not* confine the QEMU write either**, so the write reference is incus's own LXC guard, not LXD. **Scope / honesty.** Source-confirmed via a white-box review of the public repo at fresh HEAD (`ccdf811`) plus an LXD cross-reference; the guard absence was grep-verified. A live-VM end-to-end PoC is the documented next step. The read is a clean arbitrary host-file disclosure. The write is a genuine root-owned arbitrary-file-create primitive, but the created path is **forced to carry a `.out` suffix**, which constrains a direct write-to-RCE, so this is framed as **High**, not a 9.9 Critical, and no RCE is claimed without a `.out`-compatible execution path. ### PoC On a self-hosted **incus 7.2.0 or later**, craft a VM image whose `metadata.yaml` contains: ```yaml templates: '/x': template: '../../../../../../tmp/incus-poc' when: - start ``` Launch the VM, then confirm on the host: ```bash ls -l /tmp/incus-poc.out # created by incusd (root) = out-of-templates write ``` Separately, a `tpl.Template` of `../../etc/hostname` is read and disclosed into the guest config drive (`config/files/*.out`). ### Impact **Path traversal (CWE-22) + link following (CWE-59)** in the VM/QEMU template path. An authenticated user able to create/launch a VM from a custom image, or restore a VM backup, can: 1. **read arbitrary host files as root**, disclosed into their guest (e.g. `/etc/shadow`), and 2. **create root-owned files** with attacker-controlled content anywhere on the host (`.out`-suffixed). **Undisclosed.** The authoritative public dissection ([Snyk Labs: *Newlines, Symlinks, and Arbitrary Writes: Dissecting High-Severity Vulnerabilities in Incus*](https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/)) covers **only** `driver_lxc.go` and explicitly notes the VM drivers were not separately audited; no incus issue, PR, or CVE names `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`. --- **Reporter:** Kingsley Olukanni (GitHub: **babakizo420**).

CVE-2026-81499.title: Project restriction bypass on network address sets
CVE-2026-81499.description: ### Summary The network address set API is missing from the auth object project-expansion switch, so a project-restricted client can read and rewrite the default project's address sets. ### Details **Project confinement bypass on the network address set API** All six handlers in cmd/incusd/network_address_sets.go resolve the effective project via project.NetworkProject(), which returns 'default' when the project does not have features.networks set. But expandProject in cmd/incusd/daemon.go (lines 326-372) has no branch for auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet, so the authorization object is constructed with the requested project instead of the effective one. Verified against the switch at HEAD c0ca96d, which handles Profile (352), StorageBucket (354), StorageVolume (356), NetworkZone (363), Image/ImageAlias (365) and Network/NetworkACL (367) — NetworkAddressSet appears nowhere. Consequence: a certificate restricted to project P can read, rewrite, rename and delete the default project's address sets, which feed network ACL rules for every other tenant. features.networks defaults to false at project creation, so this is the default state of every project, not an unusual configuration. Supporting evidence: the sibling auth.ObjectTypeNetworkACL is expanded on the same line, and the address-set LIST endpoint filters on the real project and correctly returns nothing — this is the only mismatch found when diffing every cmd/incusd caller of an effective-project resolver against the object types passed to allowPermission. ### Suggested fixes Add auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet to the expansion in expandProject alongside Network and NetworkACL. More durably, make expandProject fail closed on an unhandled object type rather than returning the requested project, so a future new API cannot repeat this. ### Tooling and credit AI assistance was used during investigation; the reporter read the full expandProject switch and confirmed the missing object type against its expanded siblings at HEAD, and independently confirmed the os.WriteFile call in instance_metadata.go.

GHSA-3rgf-297m-775x.title: Local users can hijack VM NBD migration and disk-export sockets
GHSA-3rgf-297m-775x.description: ### Summary Incus runs NBD servers over unix sockets for two virtual machine operations: migrating a VM's disk to another server, and the disk export and attach path. These sockets were created as abstract unix sockets. Abstract unix sockets live in the network namespace rather than on the filesystem and are not subject to any permission check, so any process in the host network namespace can connect to them. Their names are also visible to any local user through `/proc/net/unix`. ### Impact While a VM migration or disk export is in progress, any local user on the host can connect to the NBD socket and read or write the virtual machine's disk as it is being transferred. This gives full read access to the guest's disk contents and the ability to tamper with the data in flight. On the receiving side of a migration it means controlling the resulting VM's disk, and therefore code execution inside that guest. No privileges beyond a local unprivileged account are required; the attacker only needs to connect while the operation runs, which they can detect from `/proc/net/unix`. Only virtual machines are affected; containers do not use these sockets. ### Workarounds None. There is no configuration based workaround short of not running VM migrations or disk exports on hosts that have untrusted local users.

GHSA-5c64-j5m6-8433.title: Restricted clients can create and access resources in the default project
GHSA-5c64-j5m6-8433.description: ### Summary Projects can share networks, profiles, images, storage volumes and buckets from the default project by leaving the matching `features.*` key disabled. Requests for such a resource are transparently redirected to the default project. When creating such a resource, the `can_create_*` entitlement was checked against the requested project while the resource itself was created in the default project. A restricted certificate has every entitlement on the projects it is trusted for, so it could create resources in a project it has no access to. The same mismatch applied when acting on an already inherited resource: the permission was checked only against the effective (default) project the request resolved to, so a client could also reach such resources through a `?project=` value it does not control. This has been the case since restricted certificates were introduced. ### Impact A client restricted to a project with `features.networks` disabled, which is the default for new projects, can create networks, network ACLs and address sets in the default project. Bridge networks accept the `raw.dnsmasq` key, which disables the AppArmor confinement of dnsmasq and allows arbitrary dnsmasq directives. As dnsmasq is started as root, this can lead to code execution as root on the host. The same applies to network zones when `features.networks.zones` is disabled, and to profiles, images, image aliases, custom storage volumes and storage buckets when the matching feature is disabled on the project. Beyond creation, the same gap let a restricted client read, update, rename or delete inherited resources, and read another project's network DHCP leases, by selecting them through the `?project=` parameter without holding access to that project. ### Workarounds Setting `restricted.networks.access` on restricted projects to the list of existing networks they may use prevents the creation of networks. There is no workaround for the other resource types other than enabling the matching `features.*` key on projects used by restricted clients, which for most keys requires the project to be empty.

GHSA-5pgx-q9xx-j3qv.title: Restricted project users can read or overwrite host files through special files, hard links or symlinks in backup or image metadata
GHSA-5pgx-q9xx-j3qv.description: ### Impact A client with a restricted certificate that can create images, instances or backups in a project can import a backup or image whose metadata area — the instance volume excluding the guest rootfs, such as `metadata.yaml`, `backup.yaml` or any entry beside them — contains a special file, a hard link or a symlink in place of a regular file. The daemon processes these files as root, outside any container confinement: - A block or character device special file is read and written as the referenced host device. The major and minor numbers are attacker-chosen, so the node can target any host device: pointed at a host block device this corrupts the host's or another instance's storage, and a named pipe makes the import block the daemon indefinitely. - A hard link in place of `backup.yaml` is followed when the daemon writes the instance's backup file, so the write lands on the attacker-chosen host file. - A symlink in the metadata area is followed when the instance is later published or exported, so the generated image or backup embeds the contents of the file it points at, including files of other projects or of the host. ### Workarounds Do not grant image, instance or backup creation to restricted certificates or restricted-project users for untrusted tenants until patched. Operators can audit imported instances for non-regular files, hard links or symlinks in the metadata area (everything in the instance volume except the `rootfs` directory).

GHSA-8r3h-vc36-6xpx.title: Restricted and view-only clients can read resources in the default project
GHSA-8r3h-vc36-6xpx.description: ### Summary Projects can use profiles, images, storage volumes, buckets, networks and network zones from the default project by leaving the matching `features.*` key disabled. To support this, restricted certificates are granted read-only access to those resources in the default project. That access was granted regardless of the project being accessed, so a restricted certificate could read them by requesting the default project directly, even when none of its own projects inherit them. This has been the case since restricted certificates were introduced. ### Impact A restricted client can read the configuration of any profile, image, custom storage volume, storage bucket or network zone in the default project, and download any custom volume or bucket backup, provided it knows the resource name. Listing those resources isn't possible. This includes secrets such as network zone peer keys and any credentials stored in profile configuration, as well as the full content of custom volume and bucket backups. The custom volume and bucket backup export routes required only `can_view` rather than backup-management access, so any client that can view the volume or bucket — including a project `viewer` and the inherited default-project access above — could export its backup and obtain the volume's full contents or the bucket's S3 admin keys. ### Workarounds None.

GHSA-f7xp-22ph-v444.title: Incus guest-API image export ignores the guest's project, exposing other projects' images
GHSA-f7xp-22ph-v444.description: ### Summary The `/dev/incus` guest-API image export handler forwards the guest-controllable `project` query parameter straight through to the image export logic, without pinning it to the guest instance's own project. For a guest request the permission check carries no auth context and falls through to the public branch, whose only gate is that the image is public or cached. A container root with the guest-API image entitlement can therefore export any public or cached image of any project it names — including cached non-public images originally pulled from authenticated remotes into other projects. ### Details The guest-API export handler forwards the request as-is: ``` cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:99 devIncusImageExport handler cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:109 r.RemoteAddr = '@dev_incus' cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:111 imageExport(d, r) ``` `imageExport` reads the project from the guest-controllable query parameter, and for a `@dev_incus` request the only remaining gate is public-or-cached: ``` cmd/incusd/images.go:4469 projectName := request.ProjectParam(r) // from ?project= cmd/incusd/images.go:4505-4513 @dev_incus branch cmd/incusd/images.go:4511 if !imgInfo.Public && !imgInfo.Cached { return NotFound } ``` Because the guest controls `?project=` and the export never pins the project to the instance, any `Public || Cached` image in any project is reachable. ### Proof of concept Code-chain verified (not executed). A container with `security.guestapi.images=true` issues, over the `/dev/incus` socket: ``` GET /1.0/images/<fingerprint>/export?project=<other-project> ``` for a fingerprint of a cached image in another project, and receives the image contents. ### Impact A container root with the guest-API image entitlement can read image objects from projects other than its own, including cached non-public images pulled from authenticated remotes. This is a management-plane authorization-scope defect, not a container escape: the guest stays confined to its own filesystem and gains only read access to image objects the server already caches.

GHSA-h2j8-4crh-vhfc.title: Incus exposes migration websocket secrets to project event listeners, allowing migration hijack
GHSA-h2j8-4crh-vhfc.description: ### Summary Instance, volume and snapshot migration operations embed their per-connection websocket secrets in the operation metadata. That metadata is broadcast to every event listener holding view access on the operation's project, and is also returned by operation queries. Unlike exec and console, the migration websocket authorizes a connection on the secret alone, with no binding to the operation's requestor. A client with event-view access to the project can therefore read the secret and connect to an in-flight migration's data channels before the legitimate peer, hijacking the transfer of an instance it may not otherwise read. ### Details The migration source/sink renders its per-connection secrets into the operation metadata: ``` cmd/incusd/migrate.go:181 migrationSourceWs.Metadata() -> {control: <secret>, fs: <secret>} ``` That metadata is broadcast on the operation event stream to every listener with `can_view_events` on the project, while the operation is still `Pending`: ``` internal/server/operations/operations.go:537 rendered operation includes Metadata internal/server/operations/linux.go:63 sendEvent -> Send(projectName, EventTypeOperation, ...) ``` The migration websocket authorizes on the secret only — no requestor check, in contrast to exec and console: ``` cmd/incusd/migrate.go:190-211 migrationSourceWs.Connect(): matches r.FormValue('secret') only cmd/incusd/instance_exec.go:96 execWs.connect(): if !op.IsSameRequestor(r) { Forbidden } cmd/incusd/instance_console.go:94 consoleWs.connect(): if !op.IsSameRequestor(r) { Forbidden } ``` and the websocket endpoint itself is `AllowUntrusted`: ``` cmd/incusd/operations.go:54 operationWebsocketGet AllowUntrusted: true ``` A restricted certificate scoped to a project is granted every entitlement on that project, so it holds both `can_view_events` and `can_view_operations` — meaning the secret is reachable both through the event stream and through `GET /1.0/operations/{id}`. ### Proof of concept Runtime-verified on Incus 6.0.0 (single daemon, privileged container, attacker remote looped back over HTTPS — the CLI-mediated migration path that generates websocket secrets): ``` === operation event broadcast (sniffer view, secrets masked) === {'type':'operation','project':'default', 'metadata':{'class':'websocket','description':'Migrating instance','id':'2689233b-...', 'metadata':{'control':'bc553c24...','fs':'2ea16bec...'}, 'resources':{'instances':['/1.0/instances/c1']},'status':'Pending','status_code':105}} === attacker websocket connection times (natural race) === control: connected +0.012s after secret broadcast fs: connected +0.013s after secret broadcast === legitimate migration target, arriving second (incusd journal) === level=error msg='Failed migration on target' err='Failed getting migration target filesystem connection: websocket: bad handshake' instance=c2m === attacker receives migration-channel bytes === first data frame = 3715-byte migration index header JSON {'config':{'Container':{...full instance config, image fingerprint, volatile.*...}}} ``` Controls in the same lab: `incus restart` operations broadcast no secret-bearing events (0/3), and the same migration without the hijacker succeeds. Recorded limitations: the event subscriber used an admin-equivalent certificate (the `can_view_events`-only restricted path is code-chain); the demo was single-daemon; and the full rootfs transfer after the index header was not captured — the channel hijack, rejection of the legitimate consumer, and first payload bytes are the captured facts. ### Impact A client with event-view access to a project can capture the connection secrets of an in-flight migration and hijack its data websockets, winning a race measured at tens of milliseconds in the lab. The legitimate migration then fails server-side, and the attacker receives the migration channel — including the full instance configuration, image fingerprint and volatile keys in the index header, and the instance's filesystem stream that follows — for an instance it may not otherwise read.

GHSA-jcw9-v2ff-8m79.title: Restricted project users can create resources in the default project, bypassing project isolation (host root via dnsmasq, host file read via mkfs)
GHSA-jcw9-v2ff-8m79.description: ### Impact Incus authorizes resource-creation requests against the project named in the request, but creates the resource in the *effective* project. For a project without the relevant `features.*` flag, the effective project is `default` (for example `features.storage.volumes=false` or the default `features.networks=false`). A client certificate restricted to a single project, holding only a create entitlement on that project, can therefore create objects in `default`, which is unrestricted. Two of these paths reach code that runs as root and give full host compromise: - **Networks (host root).** A bridge network created in `default` carries `raw.dnsmasq`, which is written verbatim into the dnsmasq config and loaded via `--conf-file`; when it is set, the dnsmasq AppArmor profile is skipped. Injecting `leasefile-ro` with `dhcp-script=<path>` makes dnsmasq run the script as root at startup (`-u`/`-g` do not constrain the lease script, and no `--dhcp-scriptuser` is passed). No container or DHCP lease is required. - **Storage volumes (host file disclosure).** A custom volume created in `default` carries `block.create_options`; on block-backed pools this reaches `makeFSType` as `mkfs` arguments run as root. `block.create_options=-d /etc` on an ext4 volume copies the host's `/etc` into a tenant-mountable filesystem (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, ...); other arguments extend the primitive. This also bypasses the restricted-project `block.create_options` check (GHSA-4cph-ccqv-hm3c), because `default` is not restricted. The same authorization gap exists on the create paths for storage buckets, network zones, network ACLs and profiles. These do not reach a root-exec primitive, but still let a restricted tenant create objects in `default`, breaking project isolation. Creating a storage bucket this way also bypassed the project's `restricted.storage-pools.access`, letting the tenant place a bucket on a storage pool its project is not allowed to use. The image-creation path is not affected; it already re-authorizes the effective project. ### Workarounds Do not grant resource-creation entitlements (networks, storage volumes/buckets, network zones/ACLs, profiles) to restricted certificates or restricted-project users on servers where those projects have `features.*` disabled. Operators can audit `default` for objects created by tenant identities, in particular bridge networks carrying `raw.dnsmasq` and custom volumes carrying `block.create_options`.

GHSA-pf5w-m8m6-5265.title: Recursive and all-projects responses disclose other projects' bucket S3 keys and profile configuration to restricted clients (incomplete fix of GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j)
GHSA-pf5w-m8m6-5265.description: ### Impact A restricted TLS client that can only *view* a storage bucket can read that bucket's S3 access key and secret key through the recursive bucket responses. The explicit key endpoints (`GET .../buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../buckets/{bucket}/keys/{key}`) were restricted to `can_edit` by the fix for GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j. However, the bucket detail response with recursion and the bucket list response with `recursion=2` both embed the full key list, including `secret-key`, and did not apply that `can_edit` check. A client with only `can_view` on the bucket therefore obtained the credentials that the explicit routes deny. This is reachable in ordinary multi-tenancy: a certificate restricted to a project with `features.storage.buckets=false` inherits the `default` project's buckets, can view them, and so can read their S3 keys. The disclosed keys are credentials for the bucket's object storage. The same class of mistake affects the list endpoints that accept `all-projects=true`: the per-object access check was evaluated against the project named in the request rather than each object's own project. The TLS authorizer skips its project refusal for all-projects requests and relies on that per-object check, so it approved every object regardless of the project it belongs to. Two listings are affected: - `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets?all-projects=true` returns the configuration of buckets in every project, and with `recursion=2` their S3 access and secret keys. - `GET /1.0/profiles?all-projects=true` returns the profiles of every project, and with `recursion=1` their full `config` and `devices`, including sensitive `environment.*`, `cloud-init.*` and `user.*` values. A restricted client — including one scoped to a project with no relationship to the target, or one with an empty project list — can therefore read this data across all projects. The profile listing needs no particular configuration and no knowledge of resource names. Nothing is written. ### Workarounds Do not grant view access on storage buckets (or on projects that inherit the default project's buckets) to clients that should not hold those buckets' S3 credentials; in particular review restricted certificates scoped to projects with `features.storage.buckets=false`. S3 keys for buckets that may have been exposed to such clients should be rotated. There is no effective workaround for the profile listing other than upgrading.

GHSA-q9fc-p923-6vp7.title: Path traversal, crash and storage pool restriction bypass through dependent volumes in migration
GHSA-q9fc-p923-6vp7.description: ### Summary When receiving an instance through migration, the names of its dependent custom volumes and of their snapshots are taken from the migration offer header and used as path segments without validation. The index header sent by the source is also indexed by the position of each volume in the offer header without checking that both lists match, and some optional fields of the offer header were dereferenced without checking for their presence. The trust was not limited to the receiving side: the sending side also accepted the peer's dependent-volume identities from the response header without checking them against what it had offered. ### Impact A malicious migration source, such as a server a user is told to copy or move an instance from, can have the target create a volume at an arbitrary path on the host and fill it with attacker controlled content, as root. This leads to full host compromise with storage pools using the `dir` driver. Dependent volumes received through migration were also created without enforcing the project's `restricted.storage-pools.access`, so they could be placed on a storage pool the project is not allowed to use. A malicious migration target can likewise steer the source using a response header whose dependent volumes do not match the offer. The same peer can also crash the daemon by sending mismatched headers or omitting optional fields. ### Workarounds Only migrate from trusted servers.

GHSA-x6pw-mh5w-pq73.title: Denial of service via a null snapshot entry in an instance backup
GHSA-x6pw-mh5w-pq73.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup reads the list of snapshots from the backup's `index.yaml`, but does not verify that each entry is present. A backup whose snapshot list contains an explicit `null` entry is accepted, and that null entry is later dereferenced while the imported instance's configuration is rewritten. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can submit a crafted instance backup that crashes the Incus daemon through a nil pointer dereference. The crash occurs in an operation goroutine with no recovery, so the entire daemon terminates, taking down every container and virtual machine on the node until it is restarted. The request is cheap and deterministic and can be repeated to keep the daemon in a crash loop. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. ### Details A backup configuration stores its snapshots as a list of pointers. A YAML `null` sequence element deserializes to a nil pointer, and the import path that rewrites the stored configuration iterates this list and reads fields of each entry without a nil check. The top-level instance and volume objects are validated, but the individual snapshot entries are not, so an attacker-supplied null element reaches the dereference directly. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create and import instances.

GHSA-xg75-xf37-cph9.title: Authentication and authorization bypass through unverified client certificate chains
GHSA-xg75-xf37-cph9.description: ### Summary The HTTPS listener requests client certificates without verifying them, so the TLS handshake only proves that the client holds the private key of the first certificate in the chain it presents. The remaining certificates are entirely client controlled. The authentication and certificate ownership checks compared every certificate in the presented chain against the trust store. A client could therefore authenticate as any trusted certificate by appending that certificate's public part to its own chain, without holding the matching private key. This has been the case since the initial release. ### Impact Any client able to reach the HTTPS listener can authenticate as any trusted client, metrics or server certificate for which it has the public certificate, including as a cluster member, which bypasses authorization entirely. Server certificates are returned by every TLS handshake, so no prior access is needed to obtain one. Appending the server's own certificate grants access to the database gateway, and on a cluster appending another member's certificate grants internal cluster access. Client certificates can be read by any trusted client through the certificates API or obtained from any server the client connected to. The same flaw lets a client renew or delete any trust store entry through the self-service paths, and affects the authentication of the agent connection between the host and virtual machines. The unverified presented chain was also passed to the authorization scriptlet, so a client could feed it attacker-chosen certificates to influence scriptlet-based authorization decisions. This includes clients not authenticated through mutual TLS, such as token or OIDC clients, which can still present an arbitrary certificate during the handshake. ### Workarounds Restrict network access to the HTTPS listener to trusted hosts. There is no configuration based workaround.
